s06.slug: TUESDAY · 8:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY
body: At twenty to nine the lobby is lit like an aquarium. The tube over the mailboxes flickers on its way out, Marcus has swung his chair around to face the Fishbowl’s glass wall, a logbook open on his knee in which Priya has asked him to record all comings and goings, and on the television inside a plane is coming apart over the ocean, as it has been since eight. A new laminate has gone up on the door.

body.title: Laminate, on the Fishbowl door
body.text:
FINAL SEASON VIEWING
QUIET DURING PROGRAM
PER THE RESIDENTIAL LIFE HANDBOOK, NO SPOILERS FROM THE EAST COAST

body: Doug stands in the middle of the lobby in his socks with a roll of poster board under one arm, like a man delivering the Constitution to a rally. “Dude,” he says, and the word goes on for some time, and he unrolls the first foot of it for Jack: a grid of marker boxes joined by arrows, a polar bear in one corner, and in the other a legend of color swatches. “*Lost.* Final season. Everybody’s coming. I made a *key*.”
“Of what?”

“Everything. Green’s the Others. Orange is the Dharma Initiative. Purple is, like, *who knows*.” He rolls it up again, tenderly. “It’s the recap till nine, then it’s two hours straight. Priya’s got the room till eleven. She says it’s in the Handbook.”
The RAZR goes off against Jack’s hip, and he gets it open.

body.text: come help me pack. i am VERY bad at it. also i have sides and nobody to be the sheriff

body: Doug reads it upside down with total frankness. “Dude,” he says. “Tell her we have a key.”

choices.text: Go watch the island with everybody.
response: He thumbs it out in T9 under Doug’s elbow, sends it, and follows the poster board in through the glass door.
“Dude,” Doug tells the chart, as Jack goes. “Your loss. There’s a *key*.”

s06a.slug: TUESDAY · 8:55 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL — LOST
body: The recap has a few minutes left in it when Jack gets the glass door open, and the Fishbowl is lit blue and moving: a man in a ruined shirt running down a beach, a hatch, another hatch. Doug has unrolled the poster board across the coffee table and pinned its four corners with the Fishbowl’s mugs, and he kneels over it on the carpet with an orange marker in each hand. His phone sits in a manila envelope on Priya’s table by the door, marked EAST COAST, where he surrendered it at six. Kevin’s spot against the radiator, where he reads orgo through anything, is just a radiator tonight.

Margot takes her feet off the loveseat as Jack comes in. “Sit,” she says. “I’m studying who sits where since Wednesday. It’s a small sample.” The loveseat’s near arm touches the end of the far couch. He sits.
“Father Jack,” Theo calls from the far couch, with the fountain pen raised in salute. “You’ve chosen the island.”
“I came for the key.”
“Wise. Pruitt’s is the only honest document in the building.” It is a good bit, delivered a notch above its usual volume, and Jack laughs at it anyway, because it is a good bit.
“Okay,” Doug says. “*Okay.* New theory. It’s purgatory.”
“That’s the old theory.”
“It’s the old theory with a *key*. They keep saying it’s not purgatory, and that’s how you know.”
“Doug. Purgatory is for the saved. Everybody on that island is getting worse.”
“It’s *symbolic*.”
“Purgatory doesn’t have a polar bear.”

Doug takes this in. He uncaps the orange, writes *BEAR??* in the corner of the chart, and underlines it. “Also, dude,” he says over his shoulder, “the other Jack’s on tonight. The doctor. He’s got your hair.”
“He doesn’t.”
“He’s got the *worry*.”

“I have a thesis,” Margot says, from the armchair, to the television. Her notebook is open on one knee. “The island is a Protestant work ethic. No one on it is permitted to simply *rest*. They build a hatch, or they press a button in the hatch, or they are punished for not pressing the button. It is Calvin with a polar bear.”
“Dude, you can’t put that on the key.”
“I wouldn’t dream of it.”

On the far arm of the couch Yusuf has *Nine Stories* open and the lid on his pen, his back half turned to the screen. “Yusuf, dude, come look at the key,” Doug says. “I’m listening,” Yusuf says. “It’s *visual*.” “I’ll hear about it.” He turns a page. “It sounds like a bridge being built by the people crossing it.”
At her table Priya has the Handbook open and does not look up from it. “Oceanic 815 went down on the twenty-second of September, 2004,” she says. “You have 2005.”
“It’s a theory,” Doug says.
“It’s a calendar.” Priya turns a page and goes on not watching.

The recap ends to a cheer that she quells with one look, and the program begins. On the far couch Theo has the blazer on and the fountain pen in its pocket, and a yellow legal pad lies face down on the cushion between him and Laney, who sits cross-legged in the Pi Lam sweatshirt with Priya’s Pyrex bowl of popcorn in her lap. They have been negotiating at a stage whisper, audible at the glass, since before Jack came in.
“A sorbet,” Theo is saying, “is a palate cleanser. A birthday is not a palate.”
“I’m fixin’ to turn nineteen, Theodore, and I want it to look like I meant to. And a harpist. A girl gets one birthday.”
“Two, in Dallas. It’s a recurring franchise.”
“Once. Everything after is a rerun.”
“Then the cart *and* the harpist. A cart says *intention*. A harp says *intention with a draft*.”
“And our next contestant,” Laney tells the screen, as a plane shudders over the ocean, “is a man in a window seat who doesn’t know it yet.”

Laney goes on at Theo about napkins out of the side of her mouth and, with her eyes on him, holds the bowl out sideways at the end of her arm to whoever is on that side. Jack, who is on that side, takes a handful. “Thanks.”
She looks round. She sees whose hand is in the bowl, and the bowl comes back against her sweatshirt, and stays there.
“Bless your heart,” Laney says, and the temperature of it drops at *heart*. She gives the screen her profile. “What was I saying?”
“Harp,” Theo says, gently.

On the arm of the couch Theo’s iPhone lights up with a text that begins MSY and a time. His hand comes down over it without his eyes leaving the television, and turns it over, and he goes on with the sorbet.

At the first break Priya starts a kitchen timer at ninety seconds, per the Handbook, for facilities, and nobody moves. Doug sidles over on his knees with the marker still in his fist and lowers his voice to what he believes is a whisper. “Dude. It’s like a custody thing. You get the Fishbowl Tuesdays.”

Jack eats his popcorn. In his pocket the RAZR stays quiet; the sheriff will keep till tomorrow. On the screen the commercials end and a plane comes down out of weather and lands, which on this program is news.

The hall window has gone from dusk to nothing by the time Jack gets back to 412, and he has eaten something at the Commons that he is already negotiating with. The Carhartt is on its hook inside, where it has hung since morning, and the hill to St. Brendan’s is not warm at night. He gets the door open on his own room and on Laney’s voice, low and fast and pitched for a room with the door shut:
“— she’d *decided*, Theodore, she’d —”
It stops where it is.

412 has more people in it than it has chairs, and Hollis presides over them from his teacup on the nightstand. Laney is cross-legged on Theo’s bed in the Pi Lam sweatshirt with a fan of printed pages in one fist, striped at the edges by a printer low on toner, held like a hand she means to lose. Theo stands at the closet door with a green marker uncapped. The double-sided board he bought in October to outline his one-act, and which Jack has been forbidden to touch since the Sharpie, hangs there on a brass swivel, turned to its blank face, though where the two faces meet at the frame a stroke of marker has gone around the corner: the bottom curve of a capital *B*. Theo takes a half step sideways, into the way of it. Kevin sits against the radiator in pajama pants printed with the periodic table and a Marisol quarter-zip zipped to the chin, so that the top half of him is attending a meeting and the bottom half is in bed. Margot has turned Jack’s desk chair around backward and sits in it with her notebook on the chair back and her pen up.
Four faces turn to the door at the same speed, and the printed pages go face-in against Laney’s sweatshirt. Jack stands in his own doorway, which is a new experience.
“Costigan,” Theo says, a full tone brighter than Theo. “My moral compass. You’ve walked in on the planning of a surprise.”
“For who?”
“My birthday,” Laney says. “It’s a production, fireman.”

“Logline,” Theo says. “A girl of nineteen is given the evening she deserves by the friends she has sorely tried. It has a harpist. Marguerite, Fresno, bar mitzvahs, and also a notary, which in this economy is a business model. Forty-one guests, a sorbet cart, provisional, and seating by temperament. Pruitt is a sanguine.”
“She knows about it?”
“I’m being briefed,” Laney says. “I’m very surprised.”
“Kev,” Jack says, at the pajama pants. “What’s the birthday?”
“The fourteenth.” Kevin is looking at the carpet, and goes on looking at it. “It’s a Sunday. It’s Valentine’s. She’s very proud of it. I’m here under protest, and I’d like that recorded.”
“That’s my desk,” Jack tells Margot.

“It’s a desk. I’m observing from it.” Margot lowers the pen. “The observer notes that a man has entered his own room and been received as a guest, which is a finding. Don’t mind me. I’m here as an observer. Of the birthday.” She writes something down.
Jack has twenty minutes and a hill. He takes the Carhartt off its hook by the door and gets one arm into it.
“Where to, my moral compass?” Theo says. “‘Out’ is a mood, not a destination.”
“Out.”
“In the Carhartt. In February. Very Ohio. Say one for the harpist.”
“She’s a notary. She can say her own.”
“Happy birthday, Laney,” Jack says, from the door.
“It’s in eleven days.”
“Then early.”
Laney’s face, which was somewhere else, comes back to cold a little after the rest of her.

s13.slug: THURSDAY · 8:30 AM · ANACAPA COMMONS — HOUR FOUR, REPORTED

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side. Then he asked me what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. I told him. He wrote it down. Tuesday night he drove Clare to her grandfather’s in Santa Maria to get her violin’s bridge fixed. Hour four was the drive home. He tried what I told him. He said he wanted the drive to be shorter. She fell asleep at Buellton and he drove the rest with the radio off. Thursday he told me somebody asked him to ask me to New Orleans, that he wasn’t going to, and that who asked isn’t his to say. His grandmother wants him at Tết in New Orleans East.

body: Thursday comes in white over the Commons. The marine layer is pressed against the windows end to end, the tubes are on at half past eight as if it were November, and on the Louisiana table’s butcher paper somebody has written THREE DAYS in gold marker, and somebody else, in a different hand, has underlined it, and a third has put a fleur-de-lis on the underline.

Kevin is at the window table with a bowl of oatmeal he is eating in measured quarters, and the corner of an index card shows over the pocket of his shirt, which he touches once as Jack sits, to be sure it’s still there.
“Disclosure first,” he says, before Jack has set down his tray. “Then the report. I like the conflicts out of the way.”
“What conflicts?”
“I was asked to ask you to come to New Orleans.” He says it to the exact middle of Jack’s tray. “I’m not going to. I’m telling you I was asked.”
“By who?”
“That part’s not mine.”
“Theo?”
“That part’s not mine.”
“Kev.”
“It’s a very small part,” Kevin says, “and it’s not mine.”
“Then tell whoever it is no.”

“I don’t carry messages. I do disclosures.” Kevin eats a quarter. “A disclosure goes one way. That’s what makes it one. You said no on *New*, by the way. Before *Orleans*. I’m not criticizing. I’m charting it.”
“It’s not a hard question, Kev.”
“It’s the easiest question in the world,” Kevin says, “when you’re already out the door.” The team-captain smile arrives at once, and he pushes the napkins across to Jack.

He goes on in the same sunny voice. He is going himself, it turns out, and his reasons are Vietnamese. Bà Nội called Sunday and again last night. There is a parish in New Orleans East, Mary Queen of Vietnam, and Tết is the fourteenth, a Sunday: a lion dance, a great many aunts, and a priest who has been told about him. “She said, and I’m translating, *If you are in that city on Tết and you are not at that church, you are not my grandson, and I will have to tell your mother.*” He considers it. “It was the last part that worked. And the fifteenth is my birthday. Laney’s is the fourteenth. Valentine’s. I’m the hangover of a holiday.”
“Presidents’ Day.”
“Which has never been a point of pride for anyone born on it. It has a mattress sale and no other traditions.”

“Now the report.” He takes the index card out of his pocket and lays it face down by the oatmeal with the pen across it, uncapped. “She asked at the candle box at noon, with a taper in her hand. *Do you have a car and a night?* I said I had an Odyssey and a box of tapers. So Tuesday night I drove Clare to Santa Maria. Her grandfather. The bridge on the Czech violin has been leaning since the Walk, and he will only touch it at night, because he says daytime is for people who can’t hear. Seventy miles in the Odyssey, at sixty-five. Hour one was the drive up. Clare gives directions in mile markers. Hours two and three were his kitchen. He asked was I pre-med, I said yes, and he said *Good. Hands.*, and put mine on the body of the violin while he set the bridge with a pencil and a pocketknife. Then he said something to Clare in Spanish, and she went pink to the ears and said *Abuelo*, in a tone I’ve filed under *do not translate*.” He turns the pen a quarter turn on the card. “He sent us home with a dozen tamales in a Cool Whip tub that I’m obligated to return, which makes it, formally, a second encounter. I’ve scheduled it.”
“That’s three hours.”
“Three excellent hours. I didn’t say hour four.” Kevin sits up. “Hour four was the drive home.”

body.text: “I tried your answer. Word for word. I had it on the card.”
body.else: “I tried the thing you said. About the drive.”

body: “And?”
“I tried to want the drive to be longer.” Kevin picks up the pen, and puts it down. “I wanted the drive to be shorter.”
Jack waits for the rest. At the Louisiana table somebody does a *Who dat?* and the waffle line answers it.
“There was a truck,” Kevin says.
“A truck.”

“A flatbed. Hay. Forty-one miles an hour from Buellton to the tunnel.” He looks at the oatmeal. “Clare fell asleep at Buellton. I drove the rest with the radio off so she wouldn’t wake.” A pause, in which he lines the pen up with the card. “It was very peaceful,” he says, like a diagnosis.

choices.key: Kevin told you hour four was a drive home from Santa Maria, and he wanted the drive to be shorter. You told him the truck counts.
response: “It was a big truck,” Kevin says. He tries the sentence for weight, and it seems to bear him, and the team-captain smile comes up and holds. “A *lot* of hay.”

“At forty-one,” Kevin agrees, warmly, as to a fellow witness. He caps the pen and slides the index card back into his pocket without having written a word on it, and goes back to the oatmeal, in quarters.

choices.key: Kevin told you hour four was a drive home from Santa Maria, and he wanted the drive to be shorter. You asked him what he wanted instead.
response: Kevin doesn’t answer. He looks down at the oatmeal for as long as it takes the Louisiana table to get through a *Who dat?* and the waffle line to answer it.
“There’s a midterm Tuesday. It’s a good midterm.” He stacks Jack’s tray on his own, and carries both to the belt.

choices.key: Kevin told you hour four was a drive home from Santa Maria, and he wanted the drive to be shorter. You told him next time make the brothers drive.
response: “There are four of them,” Kevin says. “They’d want to vote.”

The idea of four Dominguez brothers in the Odyssey, conducting a roll call at sixty-five, reaches his face by stages. He turns the index card over, writes *brothers drive* on it in his small careful letters, underlines it, and laughs at himself in the quiet way he laughs when no one is keeping score.
